items.abstract: <jats:p>This study presents the laminar technology from Late Acheulian contexts (ca. 500–300 ka) at Jaljulia, Israel. The lithic assemblages include laminar cores, core trimming elements, and laminar end-products, representing the only known evidence, to date, of blade technology within a sequence of typical handaxe-bearing Acheulian horizons. Although the majority of analyzed blades do not exhibit evident traces of regularity, serial blade production is indicated by some attributes resembling the principles of the succeeding Acheulo-Yabrudian Cultural Complex (AYCC) Amudian standards. Notably, the earliest Jaljulia localities predate the AYCC by ~100 ka, suggesting a possible Acheulian origin for late Lower Paleolithic laminar production in the Levant. The onset of blade production at Jaljulia coincides chronologically with the earliest known blade industries across Africa, appearing in isolated instances prior to the broader dissemination of Middle Pleistocene laminar technologies. Distinct blade technologies appear to have emerged independently across various Middle Pleistocene contexts, predating the appearance of Homo sapiens and reflecting innovations rooted in earlier phases of human cultural and biological evolution. This evidence parallels the independent emergence of other technological systems, such as the Levallois method and Quina retouch, indicating that convergent cultural evolution in light-duty technologies operated as early as the Lower Paleolithic.</jats:p>

items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Regional variability and long‐term changes of past ecosystems likely had a strong impact on hunter–gatherer population dynamics, including the expansion of anatomically modern humans and the disappearance of Neanderthals. However, our understanding of these ecosystems remains limited, even when looking at large‐scale patterns, such as the extent and distribution of forested areas. Vegetation reconstructions are key to better understanding ecological preferences and their influence on the spatial distribution and dispersals of early humans. Here, we compare four different vegetation reconstruction techniques, two based on pollen data and two vegetation models, between 70 and 20 thousand years before present in Europe. Absolute values in forest cover can differ by up to 40% between reconstruction techniques, highlighting that the choice of method can make the difference between a boreal forest and a tundra. Besides method‐specific and statistical uncertainties, the reason for such a substantial offset lies in the loose definition of forest cover metrics, rendering a direct comparison between methods impossible. At the same time, we show that all reconstruction techniques accurately reconstruct ecosystem dynamics over time on continental to regional scales. We therefore highly recommend that researchers use relative forest cover measures as the more robust method to estimate past landscapes.</jats:p>

items.title: Forest or tundra? How different vegetation reconstructions of Last Glacial landscapes in Europe may shape our perception of early human dispersal processes

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:list>
                      <jats:list-item>
                        <jats:p>Quantifying biological motion is fundamentally tied to quantifying the biological structures that produce that motion. Yet, this dependence makes it essential to decouple motion from static morphology to enable general, comparable analyses across individuals and conditions.</jats:p>
                      </jats:list-item>
                      <jats:list-item>
                        <jats:p>In this work, we present a methodological pipeline to study biological motion data obtained from experimental motion capture of human breathing kinematics before and after maximal exercise (gold‐standard optoelectronic plethysmography markers). We used four‐dimensional geometric morphometrics (4DGM; 3D shape through time) to characterize breathing patterns while standardizing torso shape and expiratory and inspiratory times.</jats:p>
                      </jats:list-item>
                      <jats:list-item>
                        <jats:p>Results showed not only differences in breathing pattern before and after maximal exercise, but also differences in motion pattern associated with BMI and torso shape. Specifically, we found higher thoracoabdominal asynchrony in low‐BMI subjects compared with high‐BMI subjects. We also found a strong covariation between torso shape and the 3D trajectory of motion, demonstrating the power of the method to detect a shape‐to‐function signal even with a small sample size.</jats:p>
                      </jats:list-item>
                      <jats:list-item>
                        <jats:p>This method is proposed as a flexible tool to separate biological motion from its underlying structure, which is particularly useful for studying complex systems. In the case of breathing pattern, it is proposed to investigate possible applications in clinical settings to test whether it detects differences between healthy and pathological kinematics, in sport sciences to attempt to link respiratory function to performance, and in evolutionary studies as a possible tool for inferring respiratory function in extinct morphologies.</jats:p>
                      </jats:list-item>
                    </jats:list>
                  </jats:p>

items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Sets of sub‐parallel composite ridges in glaciated landscapes have long been regarded as landforms produced by glacitectonism, the brittle and ductile deformation of sediments at and immediately beyond glacier and ice‐sheet margins resulting from stresses produced by ice. The morphology and internal structure of a glacitectonic thrust complex buried beneath up to 130 m of sediment on Egersundbanken, North Sea, is examined using a 3D seismic cube (ABP23001, area 580 km
                    <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                    ). Several ridge complexes are identified, totalling 117 km
                    <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                    in area and volume about 7 km
                    <jats:sup>3</jats:sup>
                    . The ridges are the tops of individual imbricate thrust sheets that extend below local palaeo‐surfaces. Depressions between ridges relate to thrust faults. Ridge‐system bases are defined by a decollement surface. Ridge orientation implies past ice flow from the ENE, from an ice sheet centred over Scandinavia probably during the Saalian glaciation. The geomorphology of Egersundbanken glacitectonic thrust complex, combined with evidence on the dimensions of other composite ridges from terrestrial and marine settings around the North Sea, provides a geometric baseline against which other types of glacier‐produced ridges orientated transverse to ice‐flow direction can be distinguished (e.g., corrugation, annual, De Geer, crevasse‐squeeze and recessional‐ and terminal‐moraine ridges). There are orders of magnitude differences between ridge types. Glacitectonic complexes are large relative to many other glacial ridges, often 10
                    <jats:sup>2 </jats:sup>
                    km
                    <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                    in area and with volumes of 10 km
                    <jats:sup>3</jats:sup>
                    . Corrugation and crevasse‐squeeze ridges are much smaller than composite ridges, whereas major ice‐recessional moraine ridges are often more widely spaced and much larger than glacitectonic complexes. Glacitectonic thrust complexes therefore have a relatively distinctive surface morphology and internal architecture when compared with other transverse‐to‐flow ridges in glaciated landscapes.
                  </jats:p>

items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Understanding Earth‐surface processes along the fringes of large ice sheets is integral to deciphering cold‐region environmental variability and anticipating slope instability under climate change. We investigate the Meseta Chile Chico, a volcanic plateau in the central Patagonian Andes, located at the eastern margin of the former Patagonian Ice Sheet. Here, glacier retreat patterns are well‐constrained, while the influence of periglacial, paraglacial, and postglacial processes is not. We employ geomorphological mapping integrated with geological and palaeoclimate reconstructions to provide a spatio‐temporal model of landscape evolution. Enhanced erosion since the late Pliocene, caused by differential tectonic uplift and glacial isostatic rebound, produced the rugged morphology that characterizes the Meseta Chile Chico. During the Last Glacial Maximum, glaciers occupied surrounding valleys, while the surface of the plateau was reshaped by long‐lasting periglacial freeze‐thaw cycles and nivation. Postglacial landscape adjustment included intensified landslide activity along the edges of the plateau (linked to paraglacial de‐buttressing at its bordering valleys) and regional base‐level changes. During the Holocene, flow‐type landslides became increasingly controlled by climatic variability. The geomorphology of the Meseta Chile Chico reflects an interplay between inherited geology, (de)glaciation, and climate, highlighting the importance of an interdisciplinary approach for understanding recent landscape dynamics in deglaciating mountain regions.</jats:p>
